title: The Swift Compilation Process
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of the swift compilation process in a Swift program or workflow.
Apply source code and compiler diagnostics in a small, inspectable example.
Check the expected result and identify one boundary case or platform constraint.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on the swift compilation process and the practical choices around it. Start with the smallest example, connect it to “Source code and compiler diagnostics”, and verify the result before adding complexity.
content.why_it_matters: A reliable mental model of syntax, types and control flow lets you read compiler diagnostics, predict behavior and build programs in small verifiable steps.

content_blocks.text: **Start with the rule.** Debugging and profiling should answer a specific question. Reproduce the issue, inspect a small state transition, measure before optimizing, and retain a regression test when useful.

**Work through the lesson.** Move from a tiny source file to correct declarations, readable syntax, and a repeatable compile/run loop. The detailed subtopic list in this lesson preserves the curriculum coverage; treat each item as a cue for a small example or a focused question rather than trying to memorize syntax.

content_blocks.title: Example: The Swift Compilation Process
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save a command-line example as main.swift and run `swift main.swift` with an installed compatible Swift toolchain. If the snippet imports SwiftUI, Swift Testing, or platform-only frameworks, use the matching Apple-platform project or Swift package instead. CodeLeaf’s browser preview does not execute Swift.
content_blocks.troubleshooting: If compilation fails, check the exact diagnostic, toolchain version, imports, target platform and whether this snippet belongs in a package/test target rather than a standalone file.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the snippet from this lesson file, make one change at a time, and run the same check again.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Use the compiler and versioned documentation as evidence. Do not treat a source-string check or an illustrative output as proof that a complete Swift program compiles on every platform.

content.task: Create a short verification note for “The Swift Compilation Process”: list the required toolchain/platform, the command or official reference you used, the expected result, and one limitation that you checked.
task_acceptance_criteria: Address at least one listed subtopic from “The Swift Compilation Process”.
Use explicit names and a minimal example so the main rule is easy to see.
Verify the result with a local Swift toolchain or document why the target needs human/platform review.
hints: Start with “Source code and compiler diagnostics” and keep the first example small.
Change one value or branch at a time and compare the result with the expected output.
If the API is platform- or version-specific, check the official reference before assuming it is available.

troubleshooting.symptom: The snippet does not compile as a standalone file.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm whether it belongs in a Swift package, test target, SwiftUI application, or another platform-specific project; follow the code-block run instructions.

troubleshooting.symptom: A value or branch behaves differently than expected.
troubleshooting.check: Reduce the example, inspect types and control flow, and add a test for the boundary case.

troubleshooting.symptom: An API is unavailable on the current computer or target.
troubleshooting.check: Check Swift toolchain and platform support in the official documentation; separate shared language concepts from target-specific frameworks.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every Swift snippet can run in a browser or on every operating system.
common_mistakes.why: CodeLeaf’s current preview is not a Swift compiler, and Apple frameworks require appropriate target support.
common_mistakes.fix: Run command-line examples locally; use Xcode or a compatible package/target for framework-specific material.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating an illustrative output as compiler verification.
common_mistakes.why: A reference result helps reason about behavior but cannot replace compiling and testing the exact code.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example with the stated toolchain and test one realistic edge case.

common_mistakes.why: Swift concurrency checks and newer APIs can vary by language mode and toolchain.
common_mistakes.fix: Read the exact diagnostic and confirm the supported version before changing safety checks.

summary: The Swift Compilation Process is part of the ordered Swift learning path.
Use the small example to make one rule concrete, then verify behavior and at least one boundary case.
For advanced and specialist topics, check the compiler version, platform support, and official release information.
content.solution_notes: Exercise reference answers remain in protected content files. The example output is illustrative until the snippet has been run in its intended environment.
content.run_instructions: Use a local Swift 6.4-compatible toolchain for command-line examples. SwiftUI and Apple-framework examples require an appropriate Apple SDK. In-app execution requires a separate isolated Swift runner, which is not included in this patch.
